utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. If there are no procedural matters, the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind that you the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies. Mr. McCloskey is continuing his examination-in-chief. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, could we have that -- it may still be up there --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Morning. 7937 on the organisation chart. And, General, let me get you the Serbian version again so you can look at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the court usher, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I see you've got your magnifying glass. It's a good idea. I just want to ask you about a couple of things. First of all, under General Tolimir's sector, we note that you -- that we have on this box, under Colonel Beara, is a Major Pecanac. And this is for July of 1995. Is that your recollection that -- where he was? We, I think, heard that he ... different -- different places for Major Pecanac, and I just wondered how good your recollection is, where he was in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, yesterday, during the discussions about the security and intelligence sector, I failed to mention two items. The intelligence administration had a body of analysts within its composition. The 410th Intelligence Centre that was gathering information, analysing them, prioritising them, and determining who within the system of command needs to be informed about the data gathered. This centre was located within the Banja Luka garrison, and it was headed by Colonel Pero Jakovljevic. The security administration under Colonel Beara also had a body that was in charge of analytics, analytics of information that they were preventing from leaking. It was called KOG, counter-intelligence group, headed by Lieutenant-Colonel Cedo Knezevic. I believe it was also located in Banja Luka, although I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And my question about Pecanac, how sure are you are that he was there in the security sector as you've got him marked in your diagram?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragomir Pecanac was part of a 12-member group that included myself on the 11th of May, at the time when the Staff was established. I know that he was always around General Mladic. I initially believed that he was chief of his security detail, but later Mr. Puhalo showed up, and he was on that duty, but Pecanac remained there and wherever Mladic would go, Pecanac would go along. When Mladic would be going abroad for negotiations to Geneva, London and God knows where else, he would not take Pecanac but he would take instead my chief of -- or my head of security, Todic. I believe that it was because my guy was better looking, so if you're going abroad you come up with something like that. I know that Pecanac was part of the security administration, and throughout the war, up until I went to the western front, Pecanac was always with Mladic. He did have some vices and problems. On one occasion, he asked General Tolimir to relieve him of duty he had and to put him as -- to appoint him as the Chief of Staff in the protection regiment. Tolimir initially didn't want to do it, but in the end, it took place, but then he held that duty for maybe just a month and then returned back to the security administration. As far as I know, in July 1995, or, rather, throughout 1995, Pecanac was predominantly with Mladic. Mladic and I parted under not best of terms. On the 27th of April, 1997, I went to Banja Luka. We were, at that time, put at the disposal of the VRS. In other words, we were relieved of our duties at the time. Later on, Pecanac --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic got in touch with me, and we became friends again although there was not a real quarrel between us. I was invited to his son's marriage on 6th of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and I just want to stay on this particular subject and I understand Pecanac spent time with Mladic. But what is your best recollection on what unit, sector, administration, or whatever, Pecanac was part of? You know, in the formal sense, if he was, in July of 1995? We've -- you've -- we see him here in the sector for intel and security and I need to know if that is correct to the best of your recollection or not. In which case, we'll move him out.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. Formally he was within the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know if -- would that apply for August, September, October of 1995 as well?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it would apply for the months you just mentioned, but I do know that Pecanac was, throughout that period, still together with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I don't want to go over the rest of the boxes, but I do want to -- have you had a chance to look at these boxes and confirm your recollection that the people in them and the placement of them in this chart is correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me collect my thoughts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, of course, we see all the corps as on other -- some other units at the bottom, so that my question would apply to those as well.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There, at the bottom of the chart, that's okay. I've checked that. I've made all the corrections. There were just some staff units that were not put -- staff units that were not put in and air defence. But the bottom part of this scheme, organigram, as you call it, according to me, everything is correct. But on the first document provided by you, I put a question mark next to Lieutenant Pelemis's name. I did not know that, at the time he was the commander of the sabotage detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see -- you'll see up in the right-hand corner, there's the administration for air force and air defence. And this, General, you may recall, is the -- this, you recently revised in the last few months or days with Mr. Blaszczyk. So just take a good, careful look at it, so if we know if -- if you stand by it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the administration for air force and air defence. It was headed by General Jovo Maric, yes, that's correct. However, in the period since my departure for the western front, in other words, 29th of May, 1995, and up until the end, General Jovo Maric was member of the staff with me. He was my deputy in the west, and he spent this entire period together with me. He died in a traffic accident in 1996, after the war, and he was replaced by Colonel Radoslav Pandzic, I can see that name here as well. There were not that many people in that administration. For a while, there was Lieutenant-Colonel and then later General, Miletic, but I took him into the staff, and in his stead Lieutenant-Colonel Niko Dzajo [phoen], a rocket man came but since that administration wasn't very busy because the Main Staff would go through the command of the air force in -- in all the context that had had to do with air force, and they were mainly in charge of aeroplane guidance and we took this job also from there and put him in the position of the 3rd Petrovac Brigade. So there were three people who were part of the administration, Maric, Pandzic and the third man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now as you look at this document, does it look correct to you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Even during the proofing, I told you that the segment related to the administration for air force and air defence was done properly here on the chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence at this time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 7397 shall be assigned exhibit number P2226. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This be a convenient time to raise the question what about the other chart we have seen earlier in this trial? We -- you promised yesterday that we would receive a hard copy of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And I think now is a good time, since we've finished with this one, that you -- you get the other one so you can compare them and things. I just wanted to go one at a time, and so we had provided that to the -- to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that is 7295, for the record, the one you're now just getting in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you tendered this already. I would just like to know which -- on which basis you made the corrections in comparison to the last one we have seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was the testimony, as he was going through it during his testimony. He made a few changes from what he had originally said, and so we went through the testimony and made the changes reflecting that we saw on the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means you are referring now to the witness Salapura, or was it ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness Obradovic, yes, I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So had I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document will be received as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7259 shall be assigned exhibit number P2227. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, do you recall a New Year's celebration with General Mladic? I believe it was from 1995 to 1996, and there was a video of it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could have been only 1996. The New Year 1995 I was in Drvar. I don't think it was even the New Year's reception because that year I was in Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, I will play a bit of that to see what you can tell us about it. And I'll just ask you one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, this is a clip that we have taken from P1029; but because it's a targeted clip to save time we have given it another number, 65 ter 7388. And, of course, the other one is already in evidence. And to save a bit of further time, I'm just going to take a clip, a clip of the clip, to ask the General about. So if we could start this, Ms. Stewart can handle this at 18.16.00, and we'll play that for a short time, and it should be subtitled and we will have a transcript provided to you as well. But this is fundamentally subtitled for this particular purpose. I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "[VOICEOVER]: I think that the credit for what we have today goes to the Serbian People as a whole and particularly to the Serbs west of the Drina river" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should stop for a moment. I was told this was under seal. I don't why. The Registrar told us -- told me just now that the subtitle of this document, there is something mentioning of under seal. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. I don't why either --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the -- the Registrar will explain it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the surrogate sheet contains the 65 ter number and the indication that it is under seal, CD. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am sorry, I didn't handle this detail earlier. The original exhibit that I mentioned to you had an under seal segment to it, nothing related to -- to this event. So if I could move for this exhibit not to be under seal. There's no reason it should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I immediately would agree because this -- we have seen this earlier and there can't be any reason to put it under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me one second. I just need to get this right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am told that this particular clip is connected to some of these that do -- are under seal. But this part is not. There's no reason to have this under seal, and we'll sort this out so we don't bump into something that's under seal. I apologise about that. I didn't realize the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. This specific part can't be under seal. You should move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I -- I think if we could just -- and I think it's important, of course, for the General that we don't have the -- well, I know he can hear it through the B/C/S. I don't think we need the translation. I think it is probably better to hear General Mladic and try to read the subtitles, but, of course, that's your call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please. Is there a separate document where we can read the subtitles?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We -- we don't. There is a transcript that's coming. I don't have that for you now. But it will come for your later -- for your later review, because I know I always try to do that and somehow that has not caught up with this exhibit yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we're stopping at 20.28.4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, General, do you recognise when this was?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I have seen the whole clip, maybe I would have remembered. But I assume this is the moment when the Medal of Karadjordje Star First Class was handed to General Mladic and myself. This was in one of the huts where we had our dining hall. That was the biggest of the huts there, and we would usually gather there when the group was larger. I believe that this is it. It is not a New Year's celebration. It not Mladic's birthday either. Because the New Year celebration that we spent together and on the occasion when Mladic birthday was, we were both wearing civilian clothes. I see Mladic is here in his uniform and I'm -- suspect that Mladic would say here in the clip why the gathering, what was the purpose of the gathering. But I do think it was on the occasion of receiving the decoration. What he did was he handed over the decoration to his wife and put me in a tight spot. My wife was also there and I should have done the same, but the Medals of Karadjordje and of Obradovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction, of Nemanjic.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- can be only be handed over to male family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll sort out precisely when this is. But the main question I wanted to ask you about was whether or not you agreed with General Mladic when he mentioned that the inner core of the Main Staff was yourself, Generals Djukic, Gvero, and Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he mentioned Generals Grubor and Skrbic. He mentioned actually, the chief of the sectors in the Main Staff, his immediate assistants, actually. He just briefly mentioned two chiefs of administration, these are Generals Tomic and Maric. Other than Mladic, I don't see anyone else in this video footage, so I can really not tell what meeting it is, but I was telling you yesterday almost the entire day about the way decisions were made in the Main Staff and this is exactly what General Mladic confirmed. Some ideas or initial decisions were made by the two of us at a plank in front of the hut. We used to go there and sit there for hours. General Miletic always used to joke when the two of us would get up from that plank. He would say, Us operatives are sharpening our pencils, meaning a decision had been made. What the two of us by ourselves concluded would later then go on to the Main Staff, to one of those meetings of ours, whether it was the morning one or the evening one, either one, and then I explained the procedure of how decisions were made. If it was a strategic decision, then we would call the corps to participate in the final decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And we do recall that. Let me go back to the beginning of the video to see if that will help refresh your recollection, and otherwise we'll sort that out a bit later. But if we should go to the beginning, it should be around 17.30.33.030. Actually 0032. Now, that is OTP labelling and that's not what we want to rely on here, so I want to rely on you. So let's play it from there and see if there's anything that you can help us with. Starting at 17.03.0.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell us who these people are, starting from the right and moving towards the left of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the right, it's General Gvero. He is smoking. Next to him with his hand on his chin is General Milovanovic. That's me, worrying. To the right of me, judging by the curly hair, that's my wife. To the right of her is General Mladic. To the right of General Mladic is General Mladic's wife. This is what you can see on this footage. I don't know, but, at the beginning, I saw the date the 13th of January, 1996. And now I'm actually sure that's the occasion when General Mladic and I were decorated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record we stopped at 17.14.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh. Thank you, Mr. President. Let's let it play a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I want to see if you can recognise the person that's standing to General Mladic's -- or sitting, sorry, and to General Mladic's right. You had it, right there. Yeah. Can you make out that -- and it's 17.21.4. And it's not a very clear shot.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the chief of the financial administration, Major-General Stevo Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let's just play this for a bit to see if this helps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I don't know if that helps you, but you can see that General Mladic is saying that General Tolimir is off battling dragons in Vienna. Do you know what time-frame that would be?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is after the war. This is early 1996, because Tolimir participated in the delegation of Republika Srpska in Dayton. I said yesterday that he was considered to be as the most skillful diplomat amongst us and he was part of the Presidency or actually the political delegation of Republika Srpska at various negotiations. I don't know exactly what the negotiations were about in Vienna at the time, but I know that after that, after the war stopped, Tolimir mostly was the one who travelled abroad following -- or escorts Krajisnik or Karadzic, or whoever went as a representative of the Republika Srpska leadership. He was there representing the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I think we should just keep this marked, and I will try to offer it separately once we make sure it's -- it's separated out. And we ended at 18.13.2. And -- because it will get used again relatively soon and we'll have that -- that sorted out for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7388 shall be assigned exhibit number P2228, marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, I also wanted to go -- you'll recall sitting down with Mr. Blaszczyk and going over a chart of offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 2050 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember going over the chart of offices in the -- in those proof -- what you called pre-fab buildings at Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the same diagram on both screens. And now there is another one. Yes, I remember you gave this to me during my testimony in 2007. There were many empty boxes, so you asked me to write in with an ordinary pencil the names that were missing in the boxes. This is 1995, and from what I can see here, I was really not able to help you very much. The diagram on the left-hand side where it says "main entrance", that is the prefabricated hut where the inner core of the Main Staff was located. These were both working and sleeping rooms. What do you need me to comment that I should agree with the diagram? Not agree? Or do you need me to explain anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, for the Court, Your Honours, this was the original diagram that is -- Mr. Salapura provided the Court. We then provided it to General Milovanovic for his comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, I just want to go over the circled marks because those reflected your comments. So if we can start with the left-hand side, that's at the bottom of our screen, we see a circle with an X in it, where you seem to have X'd out that Milovanovic's security and sleeping, which was what Salapura had provided, and you have put in helicopter pilots; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, it's the other way around. On the left-hand side of the circled box where it says helicopter pilots, that's my handwriting. That's the diagram that I was looking at. The right-hand side could be Salapura's. Because it is incorrectly stated there, that this is Milovanovic's security, but if it says -- I mean, if he considered the helicopter pilots to be part of my security, that's one thing, but that's wrong. I had different security. I just want to say that my version is correct in relation to Salapura's. I'm going to prove that. 16, it says, Maric. Actually, this is where the air force administration was located, and the helicopter pilots were right there across the hall for him to be able to monitor what they were doing and for him to keep them close by because they were his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, can you help us? Which entries, handwritten entries, are made by yourself? On the bottom of the -- this sketch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wrote in helicopter pilots. Something else was written there. Then I crossed it out. I don't know what was written there before. I'm not able to see it. Actually, what it said was Milovanovic's security. But my security was actually located in another room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to know which part was made by you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, thank you for correcting that. Now let's go to the top of the page where we can see -- looks like two offices and they're noted as "Mladic," "Milovanovic," and then in parentheses "(Miletic)," and then next to is "Milovanovic sleeping quarters". All of that is circled and then there is some handwritten to the left that says: "In Milovanovic's absence." Who wrote: "In Milovanovic's absence"?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my handwriting. I put that. I explained yesterday that Mladic and I used one office, in order to save space since we were rarely at the Main Staff at the same time. Then, depending on which one of us was absent, General Miletic would jump in as my deputy, so Mladic always had with him either the Chief of Staff or his deputy. That's why Miletic's name is in parentheses and that's why I wrote "In Milovanovic's absence". I would have also written in Mladic's absence, because the same thing happened if Mladic was absent. I would bring Miletic to that so that we could work together. Otherwise, Miletic was actually located in the operations centre, because the operations centre is part of his organ, the operations administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see "main entrance" there circled at the top of this. Did you write that or did someone else?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my handwriting. We marked that as the main entrance because you could -- you entered the hut from the front, from the road. There was another entrance of the same capacity down there but we considered that to be an auxiliary entrance because mostly we would use that for exiting. It was narrow. We would enter through the main entrance and we would exit through that exit at the bottom. You can't really see it. It was next to that office where there is the word "Pandzic" next to it. So we did this in order to avoid passing each other in the hall, which was narrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, to make it perfectly clear, and I'm sure Mr. Gajic will agree with me, this is one of the buildings where we were on the site visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we also see on the right side of the picture -- well, four circles outside of the building itself. The first one is written "Colonel Trkulja with another officer," and the second one mentions "Colonel Djurdjevic" and "Colonel Masal". The third circle mentions "Colonel Pandzic". And the fourth one mentions "administration of air force and anti-aircraft defence". Did you write in all of that information, all of those four circles, to add to the correctness of this diagram?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is my handwriting, and I made these circles next to the boxes, because the boxes were small, and something was already written there in a foreign language. So I just wanted to actually indicate the names of people who were there, corresponding to the boxes. It was not my intention to indicate that anybody was outside of the hut.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And so the rest of the information that we see here, the -- says "the blue room" at the top and then we see "Gvero," "Tolimir," and the other information, do you agree with it, that it is correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this is proof that the sketch dates from 1995 because in the beginning in 1992 when we first got together, the box where it says "blue room" was where General Gvero was located. And then later we moved him one box down so that we could have a room where the inner core of the Main Staff could meet. There were blue chairs in the room, that's why we called it the blue room. That began to function from 1995. Until 1995, this was the room where Gvero slept. Actually, it was his office and also the room that he slept in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you'll recall being asked this before. But do you recall the telephone extension for your office as it's marked here?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was extension 155. A military phone extension. It was the telephone of the Main Staff, and it had my name because I was the Chief of Staff, the most senior officer in the staff. Last time I explained that this telephone did play a role like a public telephone box. If anybody wanted anybody in the Main Staff, everything would go through that number because we knew where everybody was. Next to the Mladic, Milovanovic office there was an extension in the next room, the one labelled "Milovanovic sleeping quarters," and then also there was a line going to the operations centre. That is room 3. It was also connected to the building where Mladic was sleeping and it was also corrected to the subterranean command post which I explained yesterday was the room of the Chief of the Staff. So the whole operations crew, some 20 to 30 people including the courier, had access to that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2050 shall be assigned exhibit number P2229. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just a small clarification question. On page 18 of the transcript, line 22, you stated, I quote: "That it was room number 3, which was connected to the building in which General Mladic was spending his nights" or was staying overnight. Is this building on this chart here in your sketch, or was it a bit farther away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was a separate building. It's some 1 or 1.5 kilometres away from that place and it was at the entrance to the underground command post, and it was used as a camouflage, actually, from an aerial view. It looked like some kind of weekend house or a villa but underneath it was actually the entrance to the underground command post. What we see on the diagram was a wooden prefabricated hut. It was aboveground, whereas the villa where Mladic was sleeping was a building made of bricks and mortar and that's where Mladic was sleeping, and it was at the entrance to the underground command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there a basement which connected this command post to General Mladic's villa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Underneath the building there was a garage. Again, as camouflage, so that passers-by, when they went by, would see the weekend house with a garage. However, from the garage, you would enter the corridor of the underground command post, and these corridors would branch off from the main path. Yesterday I said it was like a small subterranean town. It had been worked on for some 18 years after World War II and it was the command post of Marshal Tito. They say he just spent 20 minutes there, when it was first put into operation, and during the war, his rooms were most frequently used and were a favourite place of General Gvero, because there was a bathroom there as well, and other amenities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I just wanted to clarify this, because in fact the Trial Chamber went to see the premises on the ground, on site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Allow me to put an additional question to finally clarify this: Was it possible to get from the barracks we have the chart on the screen now to go to Mladic's villa and the underground facilities but -- by a tunnel; or are you talking about a telephone connection between these two buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no tunnel. There was a natural ditch that would lead to beneath Mladic's building and then there was a sharp incline. I usually avoided taking that path but I would take the roundabout path because the incline was not so steep. There was a telephone line. It wasn't underground. It was a field telephone cable. It was a temporary solution. There was no tunnel between the hut and the underground command post. And since I can see that this is creating some confusion. I can see it is creating some confusion, this problem why Mladic was sleeping in a separate building. It wasn't a question of comfort. It was just that because of the rules, the deputy and the commander are not supposed to spend the nights at the same place in case one of them was killed. That rule also applied to when we were driving. We were not permitted to drive together in the same vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us, during those war years, what was this -- Mladic's building where he slept, what did you normally refer to it as?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We referred to it as Mladic's villa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can we now go to exhibit 65 ter 2363. And there's an English -- should be an English translation as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think there is no English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps we should get the ELMO up. I'm sorry, I don't know what the problem was. But this is an English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Usher will put the English translation on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Though it's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But you can't have both at the same time on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, can you tell us, while we're getting the ELMO fired up, what this is?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Main Staff telephone directory, updated in August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let's go to the next page in the -- in the B/C/S. In the Serbian. And the next page. And the next page. And just in reviewing this, perhaps we could flip over to the ELMO to see what we've got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we -- could we have this -- the respective English page on the ELMO. Is this the right page, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. That's the first page. If we could blow it up so we can see the whole book -- I mean, the whole page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could it be moved a bit further up?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, the audio guys -- thank you. All right. We see just a series of phone numbers there. Can we go to the next page in the English? On the ELMO. Thanks. And if you can -- we can see -- what we need to get the -- the General's -- if we could back -- back to e-court to that page in -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I'm sorry to have to make you remember both those things. General, do you see your extension right down here?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it. The second line from the bottom. Military automatic telephone switchboard with G-1. G-1 was the underground command location I have been talking about the past two days. The last line is the automatic telephone switchboard at the post office in Belgrade. Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I -- I won't go through the -- the entire book at this point, and it speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I would just offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, we can only mark it for identification at the moment. The English translation should be uploaded first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be marked for identification, pending translation. And the ELMO should be switched off. No, it's not switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 2363 shall be assigned exhibit number P2230. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Marked for identification, indeed, pending translation. Mr. McCloskey, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I want to now take you briefly back to May 11, 1992. And again, briefly, and -- can you tell us on May 12th, where were you and where was most of the rest of the -- the staff on May 12th?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th of May of 1992, I was in the Main Staff in the huts. I organised the work of the Main Staff and established communication links with our subordinates. I also drafted bulletins and orders and notifications concerning the tasks we had been issued with the previous night. The rest of the Main Staff, or that is to say, the core of the Main Staff was in Banja Luka, attending the assembly session when the decision was made on the establishment of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know if, at that time, Colonel Tolimir went to Banja Luka to that assembly session?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that everyone disappeared from the Main Staff, save from -- for myself. So I think he went to Banja Luka too. Mladic did, Gvero, did, Djukic did, and I think Tolimir did too. They all got in a helicopter in the morning and disappeared from the area of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can we go to P00022. And if we could blow up the Serbian part that has the numbers 1 through 6 on the left side so that the General can read it. And, General, we can see here that this is a -- a segment of the report on the May 12th assembly session. It's the -- what's referred to as the Official Gazette. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have before me is correct. These are the six strategic objectives. Could we please scroll up in the Serbian so that can I see the very bottom of the page. Not that far. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's an indication that this is from 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, is that correct? Is that the day that you're talking about, that you were alone at Crna Rijeka and everyone else went to Banja Luka to an assembly session?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that the decision was reached on May 12, 1992, which is on the day when I was left alone in the Main Staff. What I'm looking for, though, is when this decision was published because there is much to say about it. If you wanted me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Actually the issue of when it was published to the public is not an issue that I wanted to ask you about. If you feel it's a -- needs to be mentioned as part of your answer, of course, that's absolutely important and you can do that. But before we get there, I just want to -- can you confirm, or not, that this decision on strategic objectives was adopted by the assembly on May 12th?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was looking for the date of publication for the very reason. These are the strategic objectives of the war, of the RS. We can see that there are six. I will not go into the contents. The political leadership of the RS met for the first time with the representatives of the Main Staff. That is to say, with Mladic, myself, and Tolimir, I believe, on the 16th of May, four days following this assembly session. The first thing the generals asked for were the goals or the objectives of the war, so as to be able to define the Main Staff's strategy of waging war. We had inherited two concepts of waging war. On that occasion, we did not receive those war objectives, therefore we construed them ourselves based on the tasks we had issued us between the 11th and 12th of May, in order to start waging war and carry out mobilisation. I heard for the first time of the strategic objectives in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the proceedings against Slobodan Milosevic, when Witness Sefer Halilovic referred to it. At the beginning of the war he was the commander in chief of the Muslim forces. I also read the text for the first time on the Internet at the time which was sometime in 2004 or 2005. In the newspaper where I was able to read the text, I also saw that the decision was published in the Official Gazette in March 1993, meaning almost a full year later, following the assembly decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: While we're there, can we now, with the Serbian side, go over to the right and show the right corner. We see a date up there. Is that the date -- should that be the gazette, the date the gazette was published?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then it is even worse than I thought. The date here is the 26th of November, 1993. So a year and a half later following the decision or the date when the decision was made. None of the participants at the assembly could confirm to me that it was at that session that this decision was made. And if -- if it was, they couldn't say why it was not shown to the Main Staff. We kept zigzagging, trying to pinpoint our wartime objectives, and it would have been far easier for us to have these six goals, because then we would have been able to organise and direct the army in order to pursue those strategic objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me just ask you about number 1. It says: "Establish state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities." What is your understanding of the meaning of that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would mean that, following the Dayton Accords, state border between the two entities should have been created along the ethnic lines. At the time, the RS existed as a socio-political entity, and the Croat/Muslim entity was not put in any particular territorial boundaries. What existed there was also the Herceg-Bosna. Until the Dayton Accords, the boundaries were never drawn between the entities. Therefore, we didn't know how far ahead we could go with the army or what territories we had to abandon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May this day be concluded in keeping with God's will and not necessarily my own. I'd like to greet General Milovanovic, wish him a very pleasant stay with us. The general said he saw the first -- this decision for the first time after the war during the Milosevic trial, and Mr. McCloskey is asking him about it. Could this be clarified, please? Is he asking the General about the contents, which is something the General only saw after the war; or is he asking him about the war itself?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, this is an strong background noise when the accused turns on his microphone. There seems to be a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The technical problem shall be resolved during the break. Mr. Tolimir, I think it was clear on the record that the witness stated he saw this document the first time during the Milosevic trial. But you are now rising. Indeed, this is on the record. You can follow up with that. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, we see this is dated the 12th of May. If that is correct, clearly, the idea of a peace agreement, especially at a place called Dayton, Ohio, is certainly a long way off. So when you mentioned Dayton in your answer, can you be a little clearer? When it says: "Establish state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities," can you tell us, first of all, what are the other two ethnic communities that's referred to? To your knowledge, now, as we sit in this courtroom today.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims and Croats. Because, as early as April 1992, they had formed a coalition. They joined up forces against the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you, at some point, on or after May 12th, understand that this was an objective, to establish state borders separating the Serbian people from the Muslim people and the Croat people?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood that back when I was in Macedonia, when, on the 9th of January, the decision was made to establish Republika Srpska. It included the former SAOs, the independent Serb or autonomous Serb regions of the Krajina, Posavina and Semberija, as well as the Sarajevo-Romanija plateau and Herzegovina. Those were the regions with predominantly Serb population. By virtue of that declaration on the establishment of Republika Srpska as an independent state within Bosnia-Herzegovina, Republika Srpska was created, as such. Political bodies were being formed in the area, and this is when a paradox occurred concerning the reasons for the establishment of armed forces. If you want me to, I may elaborate on it further; if not, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me just -- and I don't want to spend a lot of time on this, as we can see a political document. But, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it possible that Judge Nyambe puts a question at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: General, I wonder if you can clarify for me at page 28, line 20 you are recorded as having said: "I understood that back when I was in Macedonia, when on 9th of January ..." Which year are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, we see that this number 1 clearly talks about -- it says "separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities." Now, the Trial Chamber, the world knows, that Bosnia was fully mixed. Serbs lived close to and with Muslims and Croats throughout Bosnia. How can such an objective be achieved like that, given that reality of how people are living on the ground? And, again, just -- I know we could discuss this for days, but could you just give us a short idea of that particular conundrum, or paradox, if you will?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although Bosnia and Herzegovina resembled and still does a melting pot, or a tiger's skin, as regards the mixture of population that pattern, still, had certain specific areas. There are such areas where the Serbs are in the majority. Then there are such areas where we have the Muslims in the majority, or Croats. Roughly speaking, in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole, there were 31.7 per cent Serbs, 42 or 43 per cent Muslims, and 17.5 per cent Croats. However, they were grouped more or less. The Serbs were predominantly in the Krajina, Eastern Bosnia and Eastern Herzegovina. The Muslims dominated Central Bosnia around Sarajevo and Zenica and in the area between Doboj and Sarajevo. The Croats lived in Central Bosnia but towards the outskirts of that area in the Lasva Valley, on Mount Vlasic and in Travnik and Bugojno. So the ethnic communities were grouped in a way, or concentrated. In the area of what is now the Federation of the Bosnia-Herzegovina, out of the total number of inhabitants before the war, there were 17 per cent Serbs. That is to say, out of the total number of Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, 17 per cent of them lived in the Federation territory. Meaning that 83 per cent of them were concentrated in the areas I just enumerated, in the Krajina, Semberija, Eastern Bosnia, Romanija, and Eastern Herzegovina. Under such circumstances, an ethnic division could have been carried out, in order to separate the communities. Such agreement was, indeed, reached in Lisbon, as part of the Cutileiro Plan and this gave hope for Bosnia-Herzegovina to steer clear of the war. However, on the way back to Sarajevo, on the plane, Alija Izetbegovic withdrew his signature. And what I heard was that Zimmerman, US ambassador in Belgrade talked him into doing so. Warren Zimmerman, I believe. Once the plane landed, no one awaited him. There were no assistants of his. Only the commander of the 2nd Army awaited him, as well as General MacKenzie of UNPROFOR. Then they took him to Lukavica and Alija tried to picture that as his kidnapping. In any case, to cut things short, it was possible to carry out such a division among the ethnic communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That agreement was reached, then annulled, and was only implemented because of the Dayton Accords. However, we were not accorded the status of states, neither the RS nor the Federation. We were only accorded the status of entities which is a step lower than a state. It amounts to some 70 per cent of statehood prerogatives in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, are you suggesting that Dayton Accords supported the division in Bosnia of peoples by ethnicity? It's a simple question, a simple answer.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We must say, though, that the Muslims and Croats voluntarily joined a single entity. It's a matter that was part of the Washington Agreement of March 1, 1994. The Dayton Accords simply copied that solution and changed the name. They were no longer to the Muslim/Croat federation, but the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we should end that discussion now, and it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. We must have our first break now, and we will resume at 11.00. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I look at my outline I hope to finish in the next -- sometime in the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, you're very optimistic. Thank you. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. General, you had mentioned briefly. Now I want to take us to July 1995, where you had told us you were on the western front and that you had come back to the Crna Rijeka area for General Zivanovic's retirement party or going-away function. So could you just tell us what date did you come back to the area and where did you go? And just tell us a bit about that in a -- in a brief narrative.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 19th of July. I was summoned on the 18th by General Mladic to come the following day. He wasn't sure on which day the going-away function was supposed to be held but he summoned me to be there, to be present. I arrived at Crna Rijeka in the evening hours of the 19th of July. I didn't find any of the Main Staff members in the prefab buildings and I asked the courier by the name of Sladjan Kovacevic, who was the senior officer present in the staff and he told me General Gvero, he is somewhere in the subterranean command post. He went to take a bath. I got in touch with Gvero, and, as first -- his first words to me were, I congratulate you on Zepa. And I asked him, What do you mean, Zepa? And he said, Well, our forces are entering Zepa. Most probably we are in the middle of negotiations with the Muslims there. I spent the night at Crna Rijeka and on the following day, we went to Restaurant Jela, which is somewhere halfway between Han Pijesak and Sokolac, the sending-off party was to take place there. Everyone was there. You have even the footage of it. We were waiting for General Mladic. General Mladic arrived from somewhere in a helicopter. We greeted each other, because I was there to receive him when he came, and then we walked to the restaurant together. Mladic was there only for a brief period, not more than 20 minutes or certainly less than half an hour. He handed a usual type of gift to General Zivanovic, said a few words about Zivanovic's command of the corps, and headed off back to the helicopter. I went with him to the helicopter. And on the way from the restaurant to the helicopter, which is about 50 metres distance I asked him, is there a way -- he asked me whether there was a way to keep Glamoc and Bihac, and I told him if can he give me three additional brigades, yes. And, indeed, the two towns fell on the 28th of July. That was my entire stay there. I went back to Crna Rijeka. I stayed there for I don't know how long, but on the 22nd of July, I was already back in Drvar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you asked him for those three additional brigades for the western front, did you get them?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got two brigades, but only on the 2nd of August. It was the Protection Regiment, and one brigade that was part of the Drina Corps, namely the Zvornik Brigade that was under the command of then-Colonel Pandurevic but it was too late; Glamoc was already lost, and Drvar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see General Tolimir anywhere around Crna Rijeka when you arrived, or at the Jela restaurant party?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether I've seen it or not. I remember sitting next to General Gvero, I think. Between Crna Rijeka and Jela, I was -- on the way to Jela, I was with Gvero. I don't remember Tolimir at all being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know where General Tolimir was on the 19th and the 20th of July, when you were -- you had arrived back to Crna Rijeka, and then the 20th, when you went to the party at Jela?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Someone in the Main Staff told me that Tolimir was at the forward command post 2 of the Main Staff. My forward command post was number 1. But I didn't know where that was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And, General, I'm just going to play to you a part of a video to see if you recognise it. I think it's in the process of being subtitled, so I don't have the subtitles or the transcript right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think, Mr. President. But I just, for the purposes, I just wanted to see if he can identify it, and it is a going-away party basically. And it is 65 ter 1404.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, we'll provide with you stills with the IDs of these other people. But I just -- I'll ask him just a few questions. 00.02.11.6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise this person?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the person. It's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We'll play a little bit more of the video to see if you can determine if it's the function we just spoke about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you remind us who that is at 02.43.2 that you're looking at that is to your right and to the left of the screen, the person sitting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's General Gvero. And standing behind him is his deputy, Colonel Sokanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're going to skip forward a --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Actually, let's just stop there and identify these two individuals, if you could. We're at 03.35.0.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is General Milenko Zivanovic. He is holding his ears. And next to him is the new corps commander, General Krstic. And we can see one part of the head of the General Djukic, logistics chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll try to skip ahead a bit to see if we can find General Mladic in his helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we just saw in Cyrillic at 18.03.8, what is that -- can you just tell us what that says?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Restaurant Jela.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, can you just tell us what -- does that refresh your recollection on whether or not this -- this footage reflects what you'd been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first in the group of three is General Mladic. Then myself. And then General Zivanovic, the person in whose honour the party was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the helicopter that we see, is that the helicopter that you walked General Mladic out to and spoke to him briefly that you just described to us?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a Gazelle helicopter that was part of what the army had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We stopped at 21.06.9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could just mark this for identification right now. I want to make sure you get a proper transcript and subtitle, and I'm sure we have one. I -- we're just not precisely sure this is the one. So we'll get back to that at a later point. This is all I really wanted to go over with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. 65 ter 1404 will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And shall be assigned exhibit number P2231, marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, lastly, I want to ask you if you recall on March 31st, 2011 meeting with Mr. Tomasz Blaszczyk of our office, where he sat with you with several original, what we call convoy request documents and asked you to look over them. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had several meetings with Mr. Blaszczyk, most probably on the 31st of March as well, in the Europol building in Banja Luka, and we were going through requests for two days, and I was asked whether I could recognise initials or signatures of Generals Mladic, Tolimir, Gvero, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 7372, which is a packet of materials that reflects that meeting. And this was done as -- as can you see, Mr. President, relatively recently so it has not made it on the 65 ter list. I discussed this a bit with Mr. Gajic, and I don't think we have a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that you are moving for adding these documents to the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if this is -- all right. An English and Serbian copy of Mr. Blaszczyk's report about what you'd said about convoy material and your meeting with him. So let go to the next page. I don't want to go over that. You've basically testified to that already. But attached to that are our numbers, ERNs of all the material that you went over. Is that your understanding, General?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I had an opportunity to see the report made by Mr. Blaszczyk during the recent proofing. And I had a comment: Miletic's name was not Milivoj but Radivoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. Any other corrections to what you saw in Mr. Blaszczyk's report?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I also went through the same reports we had looked at in Banja Luka, but I still am not sure 100 percent about initials, especially in relation to Tolimir because he would use Cyrillics and Latinics depending on the occasion but I could tell that it was his document on the basis of the contents of the document, and on the basis of the handwriting, as far as I remembered the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In order not to waste time showing the documents, is Mr. McCloskey saying that these are signatures or initials of various officers in the ERNs numbers because the difference between the two is significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, as you'll see, the General went through many of these and circled in blue the item that he recognised and noted who he thought it was, and sometimes it's initials. It's mostly initials, I believe. There may be a couple of signatures, but it's -- it's very evident from the exhibit. And I have spoken to Mr. Gajic and the idea that I would go over some examples of them so that you could get the feel how this collection worked. But, of course, they're all in e-court and they're all available for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The list of documents we see on the screen, the first item indicates a signature of Manojlo Milovanovic, marked as "MM" which is, in fact, initials and not a signature, MM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's go to page 20 in e-court and you'll see how this works, I -- I ... And it was not our -- it's -- my intention to have the General discuss the -- or analyse the material, just the hand -- the signatures or initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, General, we see this document -- and, yeah, if we could blow it up a bit. We see it's the 26th of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, Mr. President, you will be hearing more about what these documents are and getting English translations of them so that's coming but just not through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, do you recognise this document and these blue marks that are made?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can recognise the document. It bears my signature. And a correction to what General Tolimir said. I never initialed any of my documents. I didn't know how to come up with two Ms in an initial. What we have here though, the MM, this is just my initials of name and surname but not an initial. General Tolimir used to initial his documents, so this, this is my document, I -- I made a circle around it in blue, and added MM, as the investigator asked me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So that MM was just for us to know that you had made these blue marks. And what is this handwriting we see within the circle?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my signature. During the war, I signed documents using Latinics. And it is here "M," and then "Milovanovic". I always used my surname in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now let's go to page 46 in e-court. And if we could pull that -- yeah, that's a good idea. Again, we see blue markings, and we see several circles. And can you tell us, have you -- have you made all those markings in blue?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And that first elongated -- that oval that's on the top, we see an "RM" next to it. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that General Mladic received this document from someone, read it, and that he is asking for opinion by Generals Gvero and Tolimir. He wrote there "General Gvero" and "Toso". That was the nickname we used for General Tolimir. "I'm asking you to provide me with your position and opinion." And then Tolimir first writes: "Yes," Da, then crosses it out and puts in "no," but I can't see where Gvero's position is on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So when you put "RM" next to that top oval, was that identifying the author of the handwriting in that oval?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is Ratko Mladic. Ratko Mladic's initials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir. Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please clarify if this is Tolimir's -- if these are Tolimir's initials next to the crossed over "da" and then next to the words "ne". Can we clarify which initials go with what is written.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm being asked or ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm asking the Prosecutor to clarify because it's unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm quite sure that Mr. McCloskey will do that. He is going to do that. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think we've clarified the big oval. Now let's get to the circle on the right side of the document, where we see that you have written a big "R." and "M". Can you tell us what that lower "R.M" underneath that circle means?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that the initials in that circle are those of Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the left where we see you have written a "Z.T." Is that correct, you've written that blue, like you've told us before?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lower initials next to which the letters "ZT" are, I think that's the initials of Tolimir. As for the top one, I didn't put anything there. If you see on the left-hand side it looks as if it was written "Gvero," and the paragraph -- the -- the initials do resemble the letters "GM". But I wasn't sure, so I didn't put Gvero's initials next to that. So from what we can see here, it turns out that Tolimir first said yes, then crossed it out, and then put no. If it -- these -- this -- these are the initials of Gvero, it looks like he put "no," so it turns out that really Mladic didn't get anything from this, because if one had put "yes" and one had put "no," nothing really was to be gained from -- from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to P104. Sorry, it's -- no, it's e-court page 104. Sorry. And we could take up the whole page, if we could, and we don't need that page on the left. Okay. Let's start -- and let's blow up the stop of this where we see the blue marks. And I think we now see the word "da" and then the -- circled in blue. And then next to the circle, it appears you have written "ZT". Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I thought that that was Zdravko Tolimir's initials. If you scroll the document down, you can see "da" in Cyrillic at the top. Yes. And then underneath that is a text with the same initials but in the Roman script, and this is something that always confused me, because he would switch from the Cyrillic to the Latin script, and this would even happen on the same page. So that would confuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's go blow up the whole page so we can see what you're talking about again. All right. And so we see that you have circled a part at the bottom and you've also put "ZT". And we -- can you, just to be clear on this one because there's a number of writing, can you take the pen - and they'll show you how to do it - can you circle any initials that you've identified as ZT?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait a moment. The court usher will assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I circle one of the ZT?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Not the one that you wrote but the one that you've -- you've identified as ZT. At the -- if there's one at the bottom. I'm talking about the bottom ZT that you've written.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you just mark a "1" next to that.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what -- what is that inside your circle number 1?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think those are Tolimir's initials in the Latin script. At the top it's written in the Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You're talking about this specific document we have on the screen now with the marking?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document with the marking made by the witnesses would be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, marking made on the page 104 of the 65 ter document 7372 shall be assigned exhibit number P2232. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can we now go to page 60 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's start at the bottom this time and ask you about the one at the bottom. Again, we see your blue markings. And what have you circled at the bottom and marked "ZT"?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I circled Zdravko Tolimir's initials. And he wrote the word "da," yes, in the Latin script.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And that "da" is an indication of his approval or his proposed approval, I should say. Which is it? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is making a proposal to someone here for a meeting to be held. I don't know what's requested at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And now let's go to this top one. And can you just read out to us what that handwriting says in the -- in the circled part?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Deliver 2nd of February, 1995, to General Kelecevic 10.05. Colonel Tomanic 12.20." The initials are "MDj," Milos Djurdjic. He is a representative of the Main Staff in the Commission for the Supply of Humanitarian Aid which was formed in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recognise those initials from your work with Milos Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But we arrived that conclusion by deduction, by looking at other documents signed by Milos Djurdjic. Specifically, I did not recognise his initials. I don't know what it's like. But we came to that conclusion on the basis of other texts that we looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, General, you say "we." What we need here is your conclusions. Can you make that conclusion yourself, based on seeing other texts?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Very well. I correct myself. I decided -- or I concluded that these are the initials of Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you said "we," who were you thinking of?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant Mr. Blaszczyk, who went through the documents with me, because we were struggling, first of all, to find the first and last name of the person with the initials "MDj," and our first conversation, relating to this documents - and I don't know when that was held - I really couldn't remember the last name of Djurdjic. I knew his first name, Milos, and I knew his function, and then I called General Savo Sokanovic by phone in Belgrade for him to tell me who it was at the headquarters with the initials "MDj". There was a dilemma between Mihajlo Djurdjevic, that engineer who was there. And then we dropped that name because he had nothing to do with these documents and we're left with Djurdjic, and then later we did really establish that the last name of the person was Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I would offer these collection of this material into evidence. These -- having provided these examples of how this work was carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are these attachments to the record or the information Mr. Blaszczyk was writing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. They had the brief information report and then the -- our ERN numbers and then the actual documents themselves with the ERN numbers and the General's marks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then all these documents together are 65 ter 7372; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document shall be assigned exhibit number P2233 [Realtime transcript read in error "P2223"]. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's the wrong number. It should be P2232.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's incorrect. Please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 7372 shall be assigned exhibit number P2233. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have it, thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, we -- if we could have 65 ter 7395. And this is a product that the OTP put together based on the personnel file of General Tolimir which has a, I believe, a 65 ter number. So it's just an outgrowth of something that did have a 65 ter number but it is a product that we -- that we did, and we have provided this, I believe, several weeks ago to Mr. Gajic for his -- any comments or additions or subtractions on it. And I've shown it recently to General Milovanovic. We should have it in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm afraid this was not uploaded in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, do you remember me showing a B/C/S copy of -- of something I described to you as a -- something we had done, a resume?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall the document, and I wrote in pencil at the top of the document that I've known General Tolimir from 11th of May, 1992, that, until that time, I didn't know anything about his progressing through the ranks, from school and then onto his duties. I didn't know much about him. I also wrote in the information about him completing wartime school, because I know that he told me that he had interrupted his schooling, that he had left and then had to go back because the war had began in the area of Knin.
