I'm not sure that he had completed the National Defence School and that is why I put a question mark next to that, because this is something that you would need to check with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we should just mark this for identification and I will endeavour to get the Serbian copy of it. But that all I really wanted him to say at this point, anyway, and I will, of course, continue to discuss this with Mr. Gajic. There's a large personnel file, but that's a very difficult -- and mostly in Serbian. It's a very difficult thing for anyone to go through so we've just tried to create this. But I think we should just mark it for now. And I -- I actually finished my questioning, so I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7395 shall be assigned exhibit number P2234. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. Sir, you know now it's the turn of Mr. Tolimir to cross-examine you. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Once again I would like to welcome General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned, I wouldn't have any questions at all following on the testimony of the witness. But maybe I would have some questions relating to other people. But out of respect for the General, I would just like us to look at P2233. Thank you. Thank you. I apologise, Mr. President. There's been a mistake in coordination between me and my legal assistant. I would like to look at the document that has become P2233 after being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is on the screen. Perhaps you are referring to a specific page. Then you should indicate which page you want to see.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If Mr. Tolimir is referring to exhibit that was marked in court by the witness, that would be Exhibit P2232. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That is correct. According to my notes, that is page 60. I apologise to my legal assistant because he did give me the correct document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: P2232 with the markings of the witness was page 104. And now we have page 60 of P2233. No, it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask the Registrar to indicate which page and which document we see on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the moment, we have Exhibit P2232 on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this was page 104 of the document, P2233. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I was looking for this specific page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, sir, since you and I speak the same language and we have to pause so that what we say can be recorded in the transcript, you must make a break and then we will, of course, understand each other. My first question is this: In view of the contents of the document that you have read and that you see in front of you, is it evident that activities that were agreed or approved, they were agreed on at the joint military commission with UNPROFOR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see your word, "da," yes, here and I can see then that you approved at the meeting. And at the bottom you also provide an explanation why: "A representative of the VRS will join in when the UNPROFOR informs that the Muslim army ... " and I cannot decipher this last word. I understand this document to mean that you have approved something.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that is correct. And that is so in all the documents. There are initials for UNPROFOR on things that were agreed with UNPROFOR at joint meetings, and then the commander's approval is sought. This document that you see here, was it addressed to Tolimir or to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was addressed to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And all the documents that you looked at with Mr. Blaszczyk, are they all like that? The ones that are sent from UNPROFOR, are they sent to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and not to any particular individual? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. That does not apply to all of them. We found a number of documents that were sent to the chief of the General Staff -- the Main Staff, that is myself. We found some documents sent to the commander of the Main Staff. I don't remember that we found a single document, I don't remember seeing a document that was addressed to you, but there were documents that were sent to Milos Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you this because during the examination-in-chief yesterday you said that you received documents through me, so I'm asking you: Did the documents arrive at the addressee or did they arrive in a different manner? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents arrived at the Main Staff office. And the head of the office would distribute them to the addressees, and if a document was only addressed to the Main Staff then that was delivered to me or to General Mladic, if he happened to be there. I probably said that I mostly got documents from you, many of those that were related to UNPROFOR. If I received any directly, I think that I always consulted you about them because, in a way, you were the Main Staff liaison with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. I'm not going to spend much time on these documents. I don't have any objections. I just wanted to clarify the essence and the content.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document 03972, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, I was just about to ask for the document in the Serbian. Well, we can see a document here. I'm just going to read the first paragraph, just underneath the title, "The meeting of the joint central commission report." The document is of the 2nd of First, 1995. I quote: "On the 1st of January, 1995, at Sarajevo airport at 01200 hours, a first meeting was held of the Central Joint Commission for the implementation of the agreement on end of hostilities presided over by Lieutenant-General M. Rose. Michael Rose. The representative of Republika Srpska army was General Zdravko Tolimir and the Muslim side was represented by General Mustafa Hajrulahovic." And then it states, "It was agreed at the meeting ... " and it goes to say, by paragraph, exactly what was agreed at the meeting. So are you able to tell the Trial Chamber if this was the first meeting as it states here, and what was agreed at those meetings of the joint military commission where I was a representative of the Main Staff. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer your question. This document is dated the 2nd of January, when I was in Drvar. Therefore I don't know what you agreed on. I only saw this document a few days ago, during proofing. I don't know what was agreed upon. All I can see is that you sent this information to the president of the republic. Looking at the document, it seems to me to be a genuine Main Staff document. But as for its contents, that's something I am unable to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In that case, I will read out item 1, in order to see what was discussed at the Joint Military Commission session. I'm quoting from item 1 of the first meeting following where it says, "At the meeting the following was agreed": "1. To establish a joint central commission which would meet once a week at Sarajevo airport and to establish regional commissions which would carry out tasks of the Central Joint Commissions and implement on the ground the items of the agreement and tasks which have been jointly agreed at the Central Joint Commissions." That is to say, by consensus. My question is this: Looking at the contents of item 1, can you see that, at the meeting of the Central Joint Commission, it was agreed on that decisions were to be made jointly and then the respective sides would implement them, such as the helicopter sorties you just discussed?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, I can only see this for the first time. I knew of the existence of the Central Joint Commission. Before that, there had been mixed military commissions, first at Sarajevo level, including officers of the Sarajevo Corps and the 1st Muslim Corps. I know this Hajrulahovic person, his nickname was Talijan. When I went westward I see following that, you formed this Joint Military Commission. It remained in force even following the Dayton Accords for a while when I was Minister of Defence. At the time, it included chiefs of General Staffs of the VRS and of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'd like to thank you for this information, because I didn't know when it was formed and I don't know what its scope of authority was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Since we have this document before us, I wanted to read out the second paragraph, which refers to regional commissions. "The UNPROFOR command suggested that regional commissions be established at UNPROFOR sector commands in Gornji Vakuf, Tuzla and Sarajevo and at UNPROFOR commands in Srebrenica, Gorazde, Zepa, and Bihac enclaves." Can we see from this that UNPROFOR had this intention of establishing regional commissions as part of its commands?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I can see, and I'm surprised not to see Tuzla here because Tuzla was yet another safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. My mistake it does say Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... In the document, you can see Gornji Vakuf, Tuzla, and Sarajevo are mentioned. In the second paragraph of item 1. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 reads: "Our side did not agree to the establishment and operation of regional commissions within the framework of UNPROFOR sector commands. Rather, we proposed that regional commissions meet at suitable locations jointly agreed on between the two -- between two confrontation lines and carry out the tasks issued by their superior commands, as jointly agreed upon at meetings of the Central Joint Commission." My question is this: Do you know whether the regional commissions worked as we proposed? Meeting as needed at separation lines or on one of the sides in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether those commissions met at separation lines. I know, though that before this and after this UNPROFOR called many meetings at separation lines, and we both attended one such meeting in no man's land between Bratunac and Srebrenica. I know that UNPROFOR frequently convened such meetings, but in the territory controlled by the Federation, be it in HVO territory or Muslim territory. One of the chiefs of UNPROFOR, General Van Baal once called me to a meeting in the Cazina Krajina on an airport there, because he wanted me to go to enemy territory which would put me straight in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Having in mind the strategic objectives shown to you today, please look at what the fourth paragraph says: "UNPROFOR command had" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... move to the next page. Could we please see on the first page the headline. The top of both -- both pages. And in B/C/S as well, please. The top of the page, please. The top of the page, please, in B/C/S. Thank you very much. There's a mistake in the translation. In the original we see the 2nd of January, 1995; and in the translation, 2nd of January 1993. But it should be 1995. I just wanted to clarify that for the record. Now you should continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at the last paragraph next, which is the fifth paragraph on page 1.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please display it on the screen for the General.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It has to do with what you just mentioned: "The UNPROFOR's command was for the Central Joint Commission to take over the competencies of the commands of the parties to the conflict and to issue orders to the regional commissions, while the regional commissions would operate independently under the chairmanship of UNPROFOR and would carry out their tasks independently at regional level." My question is this: During the war, did we, in the Main Staff, make -- or meet with several such UNPROFOR attempts like the one when you were called to come to Bihac, and could this be considered interfering with our commanding structure?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any discussion between members of the Main Staff or any conversation of mine with different Chiefs of Staff of UNPROFOR, because they rotated, began with their proposal that we should include liaison officers in the Main Staff, but these were supposed to be UNPROFOR liaison officers. There were attempts at introducing the so-called red or hot telephone lines between the warring parties. We always rejected such proposals. I saw there were such attempts made even when Mladic spoke to UNPROFOR commanders for Bosnia-Herzegovina or for the former Yugoslavia. They always tried to achieve that. We always rejected, especially once our liaison officer Slavko Guzic was driven out of Bugojno. He was our liaison officer, that is to say, our representative in their command. They kept him as long as he was needed and once they didn't need him anymore, they tied his hands with barbed wire, put him on a helicopter, and took him elsewhere. That is why we refused to have any communication with them along command lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at page 2 next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I want to remind both speakers not to overlap but to pause between question and answer and the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. A mistake was made. A part of what the General said is missing. He is -- the liaison officers were -- the liaison officer's hands were tied, he was put on a helicopter, and then taken somewhere where he was basically pushed out. Can the General please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please repeat that part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Slavko Guzic was our liaison officer as part of the UNPROFOR command for Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think he was either in Visoko or Kakanj. They kept him for as long as they needed him. Once he asked for something they didn't like, they tied his hands with wire instead of handcuffs. They put him on board a helicopter, took him to the area of Lukavica, in the area of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command and threw him out of helicopter without any explanation whatsoever. As of that moment on, it was the position of the Main Staff that we no longer wanted to cooperate with them in terms of positioning liaison officers. All their attempts of that sort were rejected immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. It seems to have been my mistake that your answer was not fully recorded. Let's look at paragraph 2 on the next page, which describes what you have just said. "Our proposal was accepted to establish regional commissions which would work at agreed upon locations along the confrontation lines and under the orders of their own superiors ..." meaning the superiors of each of the sides. "By consensus, without UNPROFOR being the arbiter in the event that no agreement is reached. In all those instances where an agreement cannot be reached at commission level, it was agreed that the commanders would meet and jointly resolve problems as they arose." My question is this: Because of this negative experience with Guzovic [as interpreted] and with Bihac and other examples you mentioned, did we always ask that all disputes that cannot be resolved as part of the commissions be resolved by the commanders of the sides? Because the Muslim and Croat side always had proposals that were different to ours, and these had to be agreed on at commander level. Is there anything you can add to this?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This became standard practice in the General Staff. Following the first joint meeting between representatives of the warring sides, although I don't think you attended those negotiations in Sarajevo with me; it was sometime in early 1993. Then all commanders of the warring sides were called together. The meeting was chaired by General Morillon. However, the Muslim side did not dispatch a proper delegation. Their delegation was headed by Fikret Muslimovic who was their chief of intelligence. In such circumstances our delegation refused negotiating with him. To get back at me, Petkovic then refused to negotiate with me because I wasn't commander of the Main Staff but his deputy. General Morillon wanted to keep the meeting going, saying that it wasn't important who represented the Muslims because the Muslims were supposed to do as UNPROFOR decides. All in all, the meeting failed. It wasn't clear who wanted what. UNPROFOR, I presume, wanted us to cease activities and all of the sides had their own conditions, so nothing came of it. Following that, we kept fighting against UNPROFOR's unilateral decisions unless there was a consensus on the different issues. I don't know how much of it you recall, General, but the Main Staff, including yourself sent me to the talks of -- between commanders of the warring sides when the pulling out of artillery around Sarajevo was discussed. General Mladic put conditions to me. He told me what things I could accept and what things I was to say there. In your presence I told him, General, I cannot negotiate under such terms. Negotiations mean giving in a little by both sides so that we can meet halfway. If I come there and dictate your requests and refuse discussing it, this would amount to an ultimatum, not talks. Then a Solomonic solution was found. He told me that I could do as I thought fit without endangering the combat readiness of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The first day of talks was chaired by General Michael Rose, UNPROFOR commander for BiH. The first day, the talks failed because the Muslim delegation did not show up. Rose then tried to use the same argument, telling that we should keep negotiating because the Muslims were expected to do as he decided. We refused to negotiate under such terms, though, and we met again the next day. Again, the Muslims were absent. He spent the whole afternoon chasing about Sarajevo and finally, a delegation showed up headed by Jovan Divjak. Fikret Muslimovic, the security guy, was again part of the delegation, and the recently removed commander of the 1st Muslim Corps, Mr. Hajrulahovic, aka Talijan, was there. When the talks began, I realized that the Muslim delegation had no idea what they were supposed to negotiate about. When Rose told us what it was that we were supposed to talk about, Divjak stood up and he said, I request that the Serb artillery be withdrawn 30 kilometres from Sarajevo, then I added in that I agreed. I think it was quite a surprise to General Rose. He said, Wait, General, I suppose you have some conditions. I said I did, and I wanted Divjak to tell me what territory he wanted me to lend to him, whether it was Kalinovik or Romanija because in the Sarajevo area they could not reach the appropriate depth of 30 kilometres. They had an elliptic shape of territory which was 22 by 17 kilometres and if we agreed on the 30-kilometre line they had nowhere to pull out their artillery. Divjak fell silent following that and their delegations didn't speak anymore. We concluded the meeting and General Rose and I agreed that their artillery should be pulled out to 20 kilometres, knowing full well that they did not even have those 20 kilometres in Sarajevo. In exchange for that, since they were superior to us in infantry terms, I demanded that their infantry be withdrawn into the barracks. It was accepted at the meeting but was never implemented. We pulled out our artillery pieces but their infantry remained at the front line. That was the reason why you probably included into this report that we should not under any conditions accept decisions reached by UNPROFOR that would follow a failure of consensus between the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, you talked at length about some meetings with UNPROFOR. Can you tell us the date when these meetings have taken place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first meeting I talked about was a meeting between the warring parties held, I think, in March 1993. At that meeting or with that meeting, the UNPROFOR's intention was to demonstrate who the warring parties are. FRY delegation was also invited. We refused to have that -- I told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. You talked about that at length. I just wanted to know when all this happened. We need the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first meeting was in early March. I can't recall the exact date. Early March of 1993. The second meeting about pullout of artillery away from Sarajevo was 8th and 9th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Gajic, I see you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, a small intervention. Page 58, line 2, I think the witness said that Fikret Muslimovic was a security man, so from the security service, and in the transcript we see "chief of intelligence".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, could you clarify that? To which unit does this person belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All security organs, beginning with the chief of sector, chief of security sector, and all the way to the lowest ranking officers, we used to call security men. Fikret Muslimovic was chief of security service of the so-called BH army. He was the main security man of the so-called BH army, the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir. You have three minutes left before the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In those three minutes we will have time to look at document 03974, 65 ter document, we can show how the joint commissions functioned and I would also like to tender the one we have on the screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 3972 shall be assigned exhibit number D249. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, we see on our screens a document dated 5th of January. The one before was dated 1st of January. And this is a document in relation to the second meeting of the joint commission. We will not read the conclusions. I just want to show you second paragraph where it is stated that the Sarajevo Regional Joint Commission will arrange the map of lines of contact as it was on the 9th of February, 1994. It says under number 3: "Joint regional commissions will prepare a plan for establishing, monitoring posts along the line of contact." At following meetings of the joint commission, decisions were reached with a purpose of establishing cease of hostilities as it was agreed as well by the agreement on cease of hostilities that had been agreed upon sometime before.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid I didn't understand your question fully. I will try and provide an answer and if I go awry, could you please reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: May be best if I repeat my question. Can we see that these meetings were held every week, in accordance to what the first document stated. And can we also see that the central commission was issuing tasks to regional commissions as we can see here in items 1, 2 and 3. Can you give us a brief answer?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this does show the continuity of work of the central joint commission from the moment it was established onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Tolimir, I stopped you because you are overlapping again. And I have to make two corrections -- one addition and one correction. You mentioned the date of this document but you left out the year. It is from 1995. And you said the previous document was from the 1st of January, but, in fact, it was from the 2nd of January, 1995. I think now is a convenient time for our second break. We have to adjourn and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, before you continue, I would like to ask you about a reference to the examination-in-chief. At the moment, I think you are dealing with events in 1992, 1993, 1994. I don't recall anything of that sort during examination-in-chief. Could you give us a -- any explanation to that? Because I didn't understand that yet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I started my cross-examination by tendering a document dated 1st of January, 1995 -- 1995. And what I'm trying to prove is that, had this been abided by, we wouldn't have all the events that happened in Srebrenica and Zepa later on. This is why I'm trying to introduce the document in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We've seen two documents so far, from 1995, both of them from January 1995. The topic discussed in the documents is the joint commission and regional joint commissions that should have been the basis for truce. I would like to show you now the document -- or, rather --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can I please tender both of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document, 65 ter 3972, was already admitted into evidence, as D249. And now we have -- if I'm not mistaken, 65 ter 3974 on the screen. We don't see an English translation. Therefore, it will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 3974 shall be assigned exhibit number D250, marked for identification pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we please have 03971 on the screen. It's a 65 ter number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, we've been discussing the activities of the central military commission that was established in Bosnia and Herzegovina after the agreement on cessation of hostilities. Before us is now a document issued by the commands of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps dated 2nd of January, 1995. They are informing us about their activities and the title of the document is "A Report from the Meeting of the Regional Commission". In the first paragraph we can see that on that day, in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps a regional commission was -- a meeting of the commission was held, chaired by General Gobillard. And in the signature, we can see that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was represented by the chief of the corps, and we can see that on the following page, Mr. Cedo Sladoje.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go back to page 1 to see the text on page 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the heading, we can see that it was sent to the Main Staff, personally to General Tolimir. And then we have a report on the activities of the commission because the central military commission was scheduled to meet within a week and therefore regional commissions were supposed to report on their activities. Can you please tell us who General Gobillard was and whether all the corps and all commands functioned according to this same principle, at least when regional commissions are the issue? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the document, I can see that General Gobillard was UNPROFOR commander of the Sarajevo sector. I haven't met him personally. Furthermore, I can see from the document that the regional commission is reporting to you, who was the representative of the Main Staff in the central commission. I did know some of the Sector Sarajevo commanders, Soubirou, for instance, then a Russian officer, I think he was Chief of Staff, either a Russian or a Ukrainian Demurenko. I haven't seen any other documents by any other regional commissions. I'm expecting to see them. But this document demonstrates that the regional commissions, that our representatives in the regional commissions were reporting to you personally, because you were our representative in the central commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please read the sixth paragraph from the top, the first word is: "After a lengthy discussion and attempts by the Muslim side to avoid specifying conditions for abiding by the agreement, finally it was agreed that the Muslim side -- forces will return -- will withdraw from the demilitarised zone by the 1200 hours on the 4th January 1995. General Gobillard and his staff will carry out an inspection of the demilitarised zone in the afternoon hours on the 4th of January, 1995. At the following meeting of the regional commission on the 5th of January, 1995, UNPROFOR will submit a report and agreement will be made about when the inspection of the demilitarised zone will be carried out by the joint commission." Could you tell me which demilitarized zone is discussed here, on the basis of the report, and whether what had been agreed with the cessation of hostilities at the meeting of the regional commission in Sarajevo was abided by?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to, General, but I cannot answer your question. I wasn't present, first of all. Secondly, I wasn't familiar with the functioning of the central commission. I can only say that this document is a valid document. It is in keeping with the regulations and the laws. I cannot speak to the facts presented in the document, whether they are correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. General, can we please read the last paragraph of the document, or on this page. "Our delegation insisted that the agreement reached on the 14th of August 1993 is fully abided by because that would make sure not only that the Muslim forces would withdraw from the demilitarized zone but also from the areas to the east of the demilitarized zone to the west border of the demilitarized zone that was determined on the 14th of August, 1993."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... still listening to the translation. Please slow down. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "Karavelic tried to make it possible that we carry out demilitarization of the demilitarized zone, that only UNPROFOR can do that." Can you, on the basis of the document, tell us which demilitarized zone this is referring to, and whether the Muslims actually implemented what was agreed upon, and were they ready to make sure that the Serbs can act also in accordance to the agreement. Do you remember what this is all about at all?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the document itself, I cannot tell you what the delimitations of this zone were. I can only assume that this was an area surrounding Sarajevo. But I don't know the borders of the zone. I can comment, nevertheless, on the positions of the Muslim side. Earlier, when we were trying to delineate the safety zones or demilitarized zones for which agreements had been signed by the commanders of the warring parties, which is in the keeping with the Geneva Conventions, and I'm talking about Srebrenica, Zepa, and, later, Gorazde, where the two warring parties' commanders signed an agreement, on that occasion, they agreed that UNPROFOR would guarantee whether the zones had been or had not been demilitarised. Both for Srebrenica and Zepa, because I'm familiar with those two, we believed UNPROFOR's trick, their ruse. There was even a joint commission that was tasked with determining whether Srebrenica was demilitarised or not, and they reported to us that Muslims handed over, I think, 900 barrels in Zepa and 1200 barrels in Srebrenica. The mixed commission tried to verify the information received from UNPROFOR. It was possible at the time. But -- and, yes, these barrels were found, but it was obsolete weapons, improvised weapons that we used to call "fear of Serbs". It was something made provisionally by using lead pipes, and it could have been used only once. We -- from October 1994, we did not recognise it anymore, because, on that day, the UN Security Council declared another three safe areas, Tuzla, Sarajevo, and Bihac. We were informed by UNPROFOR that the 5th Muslim Corps was disarmed, that all of three brigades that made up the corps were disarmed. We did not verify that. However, a year and a half later, the 5th Muslim Corps attacked the VRS from the very demilitarized zone. There was about 22.000 troops grouped into eight or nine brigades, and at their disposal they had state-of-the-art infantry weapons. It was the first time when I saw Singapore rifles in use. In other words, UNPROFOR lied to VRS when saying that they were disarmed because, in the meantime, the corps was additionally armed, trained, and replenished. So we stopped believing UNPROFOR, and we insisted whenever there were local agreement on either demilitarization or cessation of hostilities, that we should participate on that, as you can see the Muslims were against it, because they believed that UNPROFOR will confirm whatever they tell them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document. It is relevant in relation to events in Sarajevo later on, and the offensive in Sarajevo later on, because it involves supply of weapons to the Muslims in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 3971 shall be assigned exhibit number D251, marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we see now in e-court 65 ter 003970. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And while we're waiting - we'll see it in a moment - this is a document by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska of the 2nd of January, 1995, sent to the Sarajevo UNPROFOR command. I signed the document, and it refers to the document that the Prosecutor showed when we were comparing initials on the document where I had written "no." And let us look to the first quote: "At a meeting of the Joint Central Committee held on 1 January 1995 at the Sarajevo airport it was not agreed that UNPROFOR aircrafts and personnel would travel unannounced and without permission from the party on whose territory they would be travelling." Item 5 of the agreement on a complete cease of all enemy activities signed on 31st December 1994 provides for the free movement of UNPROFOR according to the relevant procedure which implies prior notification and permission of movement." My question is: Did we, or the Main Staff - I apologise for saying "we" - always take care to respect all of the agreements that were relevant in a given situation and in respect of a given activity; and did it always inform UNPROFOR about it, as I did in this document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the duty of all members of the Main Staff, in all contacts, either with UNPROFOR or with representatives of the warring sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document so that we could call up the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 3970 shall be assigned exhibit number D252. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at D77. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We're about to see the document that refers to the principles for freedom of movement. The document was signed by UNPROFOR and the Main Staff and it's dated 1st of January, 1995, precisely at the time when the cease-fire and cessation of hostilities were being set. Can we now look at the first paragraph of this document on the principles for freedom of movement. "These principles define the appropriate procedures regarding freedom of movement, as stated in paragraph 5 of the agreement on the complete cessation of hostilities signed on the 31st of December, 1994. These principles specifically refer to UNPROFOR movements on Serb-held territory."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at item 5 that this item 1 refers to which states, I quote, item 5 from this agreement which is on the following page. Thank you. Can the witness please be shown the following page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Item 5 refers to aircraft: "UNPROFOR helicopters will enjoy freedom of movement after notification on the announced and approved route of flying. There will be a check on the ground on -- at an agreed location." This agreement was signed in Lukavica on 31st of January 1995 by General Brinkman and Major-General Zdravko Tolimir. My question to the witness is: Did we always not try to respect all procedures agreed on with UNPROFOR about the movement of their aircraft and that we prevented that when the framework of the agreement was violated?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state with full responsibility that the Army of Republika Srpska always respected the agreement -- rather, those agreements, which I cannot say specifically for the UNPROFOR generals. They often violated deadlines or sought something that was not permissible, even according to our regulations. Again, I have to mention General Van Baal. Once he asked me for permission to transfer by helicopter to Gorazde 80 litres of fuel. The Gorazde enclave. I answered that I cannot approve that because our regulations do not allow the transport of fuel in aircraft outside of the actual fuel tanks of the aircraft. He got angry with me, thinking that I -- I was not willing to allow him to transport fuel. Then I said, All right, General, you can transport it, but let that be at your own responsibility. And this is what I wrote down that they can transport the fuel with the responsibility for that being borne by the UNPROFOR command, wishing to avoid the helicopter from blowing up in the air or something. Other than that, UNPROFOR did not respect all the agreements. I think setting off from the position of the stronger party. They did not respect the required prior announcement times. This was always cut short. They didn't respect the bills of lading that -- of cargos that were being transported into the enclaves. They would send us a list of material. The check-point - I can see here, that you had agreed that there would be only one check-point at the -- in the territory of Republika Srpska - would find something completely different, then we would turn them back. We would stop them, they would be accusing us of this and that. So looking at this document, General, sir, you are correct, and as far as those who are not correct are concerned they can seek clarification, if they are interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right, General. Thank you. Can we now again look at that document P223 [as interpreted] and can we see page 46 of that document. After that, we're going to look at page 60, just so that we can see that we are talking about agreed-upon procedures. Thank you. And when you see the contents of the document, you are going to give us your comment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Tolimir, are you referring to the document P2233?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. P2233, page 46. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We are looking at the document now. And we can see that a helicopter flight is sought to be approved, and Gvero's end approval and my approval are being asked for. I said yes because this was agreed upon at the joint military commission. But here where it says "no," those are not my initials there. My initials are next to the word "da," yes, and then somebody crossed it out. So can we see here that I did approve and proposed to the commander of the Main Staff that these things be approved, pursuant to what was agreed at the joint commission? And did we not, the two of us, you and I, always agree to respect the agreements made with UNPROFOR because this was something that was decided during our joint meetings and this was something that was agreed at that time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Tolimir, before we receive the answer of the witness, I have a problem with the way you are putting this question to the witness. If you reflect on the words you have used, it is more testimony of a witness but you are not testifying here in the courtroom. You may ask the witness if he would agree to something, but this was slightly different, the way you put this -- your knowledge about this document to the witness. Please bear that in mind for future questions. Sir, would you please answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I can re-phrase the question because we were talking about the situation and not about how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that was -- it was just kind of guidance, and that's fine. You should bear that in mind for future questions. And now, the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this document was shown to me. It was on the screen during the examination-in-chief, and it was unclear to whom this "no" belongs to. I assume that the initials are those of Milan Gvero, who crossed out your "yes" -- well, that is in keeping with the agreement made at the central commission, that "yes" of yours. But the "no" was probably done out of lack of information or ignorance and you had offices next to each other, so I don't know why you didn't agree on it. I don't know who crossed out your "yes." There are two options: One, that it was General Mladic who crossed it out when he saw Gvero's "no". Because if you remember, I said today that Mladic did not get anything from your opinion. One was for and one was against. So he was in the same dilemma that he was in before he got the document back. So I can just assume that this "no" was crossed out by Gvero automatically, which he did not have the right to do. I can conclude also that perhaps Mladic crossed it out, that he preferred Gvero's "no," that the mission is not approved, and, as you know, Mladic obvious had the habit of taking revenge on those who were not sticking to agreements. So if UNPROFOR was not sticking to agreements then Mladic probably was more inclined to Gvero's "no" than to your "yes". But all of these are just assumptions. I shouldn't be speculating. I was not an eye-witness. So all of this you can just simply consider as being left without an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's look at the upper left-hand side corner of the document to see what it says. And does it say, "on the approval of commander"? Has this been implemented in keeping with the commander's decision, in your view.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, it is true that in the Latin script it says, "yes, on commander's approval." I believe that this is your handwriting. But the initials resemble Mladic's. And yet the pen seems to be the same. It is confusing, to say the least. You are best placed to tell us whether this is, indeed, your handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, since I cannot put such proposals before this Chamber, I would simply kindly ask you to pick up a red pen to circle "yes" and the note, because the note was not translated.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you want me to circle this "yes" and "on commander's approval"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait. The court usher will assist you before you try to mark it. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just want to make sure the General understands that we are always open for agreement on facts and I think at any point in time that can be done. The General can agree without having to testify whether something is his initials or whether he did something, in my view, as long as he doesn't go into testimonial situations. So if that is what he wants to do, we are open to that. And, of course, that is appropriate in this system, as -- as I know Mr. Gajic knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, this is an invitation to negotiate about agreed facts. Sir, would you now please encircle what Mr. Tolimir asked you. He asked you to circle "yes" in the note. Below the word "yes."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please place "MM" next to it so that we would know it was you. Place the initials on the circle you drew, not on the contents.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, I wanted to state that General Milovanovic merely circled something that was written by someone else. The words are "yes, on commander's approval."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next have P2233 again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please, first are you tendering the document with the marking?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document with the marking will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 46 of Exhibit P2233 shall be assigned exhibit number D253. Just for clarification, page was marked by the witness in court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we do have the originals of these, that, as you recall that the General had actually seen when he made his markings and sometimes the different ink colour comes out in those. So I will those available. I mean, we are about to end, just so the General and Mr. Gajic know, we will try to make those available because that may add to what is being testified to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have page 60 of the document P2233. Thank you. We'll go through it quickly because we have seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see it now. You marked something. The upper note, was it written by the person who implemented the obligations of the VRS regarding the announcement of this helicopter flight which was also supposed to include a VRS representative from Titov Drvar?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand the question at all. Please rephrase it. Are you asking me whether the handwriting is the same as on the previous document? I'm sorry, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll be happy to. I'm not interested in the handwriting, because I do not dispute handwritings and signatures. I'm only interested in the contents. Looking at the contents, is it clear that the helicopter was supposed to land in Drvar to pick up a VRS representative? And was it announced, there was a Colonel Tomanovic in question, I believe, and was the helicopter to continue to Banja Luka? It doesn't matter who rode it.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Kelecevic learned of this at 10.05, and Colonel Tomanovic was informed at 12.20.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Thank you, Aleksandar. I thought it says 12.05 next to Kelecevic's name, but it doesn't matter whether it's a 10 or a 12. I accept what you say. Could we look at the bottom of the document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is there an English translation available? There is no English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, can you see that, underneath your marking, it reads: "The meeting was arranged in Titov Drvar" -- it's supposed to land in Drvar on a playground. And Pandzic is supposed to determine the coordinates. Does this mean that the arrangement on the landing of the helicopter was implemented and was the agreement with UNPROFOR honoured as such, and is that the reason why the document was initialed by the commander? I'll reformulate. In this proposal, which you said was mine, does it read: "The meeting is arranged. They are to land in Titov Drvar on a playground, and Pandzic is supposed to determine the coordinates." Was this a proposal made to the commander as to what was agreed on?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, now we have a problem. The document was tendered by the Prosecution for the purpose of identifying initials and signatures and handwritten -- and handwriting but not for the content. If you are going to deal with the content of these documents, we need an English translation. Otherwise, we will not understand the content of it. So I would kindly ask you to tender these documents, again, as a Defence document, and we will then decide if it should be marked for identification, pending translation, so that we have a full picture of that. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I do intend to have these fully translated so that you can see the content. Because content, you know, could be important. I just was not planning on having this witness, through direct, talk about content, but content is -- does have relevance and is important, and we will endeavour to get these translated, the ones where the General has -- has marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I would like to invite both parties to negotiate about the best way to deal with the translation issue. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, these are OTP documents. We do not have English translations. We have not received them. They did not receive them either. The OTP probably believes -- these important -- documents to be important because they offered so many of them for tendering and because they introduced certain markings that the witness made regards the initials. We have a few more questions about the contents, about the document. Hopefully it won't be too long, but we will need another 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We must adjourn for the day because we are at the end of today's hearing. We -- Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We accept your proposal, and we propose that it be tendered on behalf of the Defence as well, regards the contents. Because the initials are not a pure formality. They always have to be read within the context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, I would like to invite both parties to negotiate about the translation issue. We come back to this problem tomorrow because we have to continue with the cross-examination with this witness tomorrow. Could you indicate how much time you will need during your further examination, cross-examination? Because we received different messages at the beginning of cross-examination and now by Mr. Gajic. What is your estimation? I think it is necessary for the Prosecution to plan the further witnesses. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, a small correction. I wanted to say that we will take some 20 minutes on these documents but we will need more time than that for other matters as well. If I may quickly consult with the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This time I want to ask the witness as well, since this is the last day before the weekend except tomorrow. If he really needs to go home, I will adjust my questions accordingly. We prepared our examination based on the Prosecutor's estimate, according to which, he was to examine the witness for three days. If the witness wishes to go home tomorrow, so as not to spend the weekend in The Hague, I will adjust my questions accordingly, so as to allow for some time for the Prosecutor as well, if they want to examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To clarify the situation, the Prosecution had indicated 12 hours. They used in fact four hours and 55 minutes. That means nearly five hours, quite less than indicated earlier. You have used, up to now, one hour and 22 minutes. It is your right to cross-examine and I just wanted to inquire your estimation for the time you will need for the witness. This is important for planning purposes. We have the full day tomorrow. And the Prosecution has the right to re-examine the witness. Do you need the full session tomorrow or what is your position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I can tell you, but I would like to take the witness's opinion into account. If he wishes to leave, I will cut my questions short tomorrow and conclude my cross-examination, and then I will use another witness to introduce some questions I had prepared, according to the time estimate by the Prosecution. I would kindly ask for the witness to state his position for me to be able to give you my estimate so that we can conclude with him tomorrow safely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I appreciate to get an answer from the witness, but, to make it very clear, it is the obligation of the witness to stay here as long as he is needed for cross-examination and re-examination. Mr. Milovanovic, what are your plans and obligations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as I'm concerned, there is no time limitation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We adjourn now, and we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 19th day of May, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.53 p.m.,
